title.en: Dimna's Slander: The Lion and the Ox

region.en: Court of the lion-king, India of the fable (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寓言印度的獅王之廷（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah, Arabic by Ibn al-Muqaffa' (d. 759), from Persian; English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'Story of the Lion and the Ox'

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The lion-king befriends the ox Shanzabah, and the jackal Dimna, jealous of the newcomer's favour, whispers to each that the other plots against him. The friends are set at variance; the ox is killed in the quarrel; and the king, discovering the treachery, judges Dimna by the law of the beasts. The frame-story of the whole book: the philosopher Bidpai tells the tale to a king of India to warn him of tale-bearers.
summary.zh: 獅王善待公牛尚扎巴；豺狼迪姆奈嫉其新寵，向雙方各進讒言。二友失和；公牛死於爭端；獅王發現其奸，依獸法審判迪姆奈。全書框架故事：哲人白得巴向印度之王講述此篇，以警讒言者。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable transmitted through Arabic (Kalilah wa-Dimnah) and long used in Islamic education; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation of the Syriac version.

passages.text: The lion-king took the ox Shanzabah into his friendship, and the jackal Dimna, who had served the king before him, grew jealous of the newcomer's favour. He went first to the ox and said: 'The king means to eat thee.' Then he went to the king and said: 'The ox has said among the beasts that he will take thy kingdom.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'Story of the Lion and the Ox'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The friends were set at variance, and the ox was slain in the quarrel that the tale-bearer had made. The king discovered the treachery, and judged Dimna according to the law of the beasts; and the philosopher Bidpai, in the frame of the book, tells the story to a king of India: 'The tale-bearer is the wolf between two friends; and the throne that listens to him loses both.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.

title.en: The War of the Owls and the Crows

region.en: Owl fortress on a mountain, India of the fable (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寓言印度的山上貓頭鷹堡（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'The Owls and the Crows'

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The owls have beaten the crows for years, because the crows cannot see by night. A young crow volunteers a desperate counsel: let him go over to the owls and be received as a deserter. He lives among them, learns the way to their fortress, gathers straw, and in the day sets fire to it while the owls sleep — and the war is ended in one morning. The moral: the counsel of the desperate is the sword of the desperate.
summary.zh: 貓頭鷹多年壓制烏鴉，因烏鴉夜不能視。一隻年輕烏鴉獻苦計：假投誠混入鴞群。他與之同住，探得其堡之路，積聚乾草；白晝鴞群酣睡時縱火——一晨之間戰爭終結。寓意：絕望者的計謀即絕望者的劍。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: The owls had beaten the crows for years, for the crows could not see by night and the owls came against them in the dark. A young crow stood up among the council and volunteered a desperate counsel: 'Let me go over to the owls and be received as a deserter, and I will learn the way to their fortress.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'The Owls and the Crows'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He lived among the owls, and won their trust, and saw the fortress in which they slept by day. He gathered straw and laid it at the mouth of the cave; and one morning, while the owls slept, he set fire to the straw, and the war of the owls and the crows was ended. And the moral is of the counsel that is given only by him who is willing to be the fire.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.

region.zh: 寓言的河岸（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'The Tortoise and the Ape'

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The ape and the tortoise are friends in the season of the flood; the ape is carried on the tortoise's back to an island, and in pride of his rescue mocks his preserver: 'Thy kind are but shells upon the sand.' The friendship is broken at a word, and both are lost in the next flood. The moral: the tongue that repays kindness with scorn breaks the boat that carries it.
summary.zh: 洪水季節猿與龜為友；龜載猿至島上；猿得救而傲，嘲其恩人：『你們一族不過沙上之殼。』一言友誼即斷，二人皆喪於下次洪水。寓意：以輕蔑報恩之言，自斷所乘之舟。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: In the season of the flood the ape and the tortoise were friends, and the tortoise carried the ape on his back to an island of safety. In pride of his rescue the ape mocked his preserver: 'Thy kind are but shells upon the sand.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'The Tortoise and the Ape'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The friendship was broken at a word; and when the next flood came, both were lost — for the tortoise would not carry again, and the ape could not swim. The moral of the tale is of the tongue that repays kindness with scorn, and breaks the boat that carries it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ring-Dove and the Fowler's Net

region.zh: 寓言的森林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'Story of the Ring-dove'

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: A ring-dove and her company are caught in the fowler's net; she lifts the net on her wings and flies with them all to the mouse's hole, and the mouse gnaws the strings and frees them one by one. The moral is spoken by the mouse: 'They who bear one another's burdens escape the net; they who peck at one another stay in it.'
summary.zh: 一斑鳩與同伴陷入捕鳥者羅網；她張翅舉網，攜眾飛至鼠洞；鼠逐一齧斷繩索而釋之。寓意出自鼠口：『彼此共負重軛者脫網；彼此相啄者困於網中。』

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: A ring-dove and her company were caught in the fowler's net; and she lifted the net on her wings and flew with them all, dragging it to the hole of the mouse. The mouse gnawed the strings and freed them one by one, saving herself the last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'Story of the Ring-dove'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The moral is spoken by the mouse: 'They who bear one another's burdens escape the net; they who peck at one another stay in it.' And the tale is told in the frame of the book as the counsel of unity to the king's court.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.

texts.period: Kalilah wa-Dimnah (Arabic, 8th c.); English: I. G. N. Keith-Falconer, 1885, public domain

source.work: Kalilah and Dimnah, or The Fables of Bidpai, trans. I. G. N. Keith-Falconer (Cambridge, 1885), 'Dimnah's Defence'

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1885; Arabic original 8th century)

summary.en: The jackal Dimna, accused of the ox's death, defends himself with a whole day of eloquence: he cites the law, the precedent of the wolves, the necessity of the state — and the assembly is nearly persuaded. Then the witnesses speak, and the sentence falls. The chapter is a satire on the advocate's art: the voice that can make wrong sound like justice.
summary.zh: 豺狼迪姆奈因公牛之死受審，以一整日雄辯自衛：引法度、援狼之先例、陳國家之需——眾幾乎被說服。繼而證人發言，判決落定。此章諷刺辯護術：能使非義聽似公義之聲音。

sensitivity.note: Mirror-for-princes fable; paraphrased from the public-domain Keith-Falconer translation.

passages.text: The jackal Dimna, accused of the ox's death, defended himself with a whole day of eloquence: he cited the law, and the precedent of the wolves, and the necessity of the state, and the mercy that the king had shown to him who had only served him; and the assembly of the beasts was nearly persuaded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885), 'Dimnah's Defence'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the witnesses spoke, and the sentence fell; and the chapter is a satire on the advocate's art — the voice that can make wrong sound like justice — and a warning to the king's court of the tale-bearer at its own gate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Kalilah and Dimnah (Keith-Falconer 1885); not verbatim.
